concept: Apple silicon memory bandwidth and decode speed by chip

facts.text: M3 Pro and the binned M3 Max cut bandwidth versus M2 (150 vs 200; 300 vs 400). M4 Pro restored 273; M4 Max binned 410 / 546.
M5 Pro 307 and M5 Max 460/614 are only 12% above M4 Pro and M4 Max, so decode gains there are small; Apple's "4x AI" claims are prefill (prompt processing).

M5 Ultra (announced 2026-08-25, shipped 2026-09-22; 512GB config late October) raises the Ultra tier from 819 to ~1.2 TB/s. First measured llama.cpp result (Sept 30 2026): Q4_0 tg128 179.10, F16 73.60, pp512 5207.
M6 (Mac mini, 2 nm) has 170 GB/s and decodes 7B Q4_0 at 35.74 tok/s, about 12% above M5 base.

Context length erodes decode: M3 Ultra Qwen 32B Q4 goes 31.2 (1K) -> 19.0 (32K) -> 8.5 (128K); F16 goes 10.4 -> 5.5. At 128K Q2 is only 1.7x F16 (4.6x at 1K) because the FP16 KV cache dominates bandwidth.

Prefill is compute-bound and quant-independent: Llama 405B TTFT is ~37-42 s at 1K and ~10 min at 16K regardless of Q2/Q4/Q8 on M3 Ultra (~54 TFLOPS FP16). MLX prefill throughput dropped 345 -> 154 tok/s from 1K to 128K.

Batching converts the workload from bandwidth-bound to compute-bound: vllm-mlx on M5 Max 128GB, Qwen3-8B-4bit: single stream 87 tok/s, aggregate 215 tok/s at 15 concurrent (2.6x) while per-request decode falls to 16 tok/s.
Binned chips: check the GPU-core bin. A 32-core M5 Max has 460 GB/s, a 40-core 614 GB/s; M4 Max 410 vs 546; M3 Max 300 vs 400.
Power: Low Power Mode can roughly halve inference speed; High Power Mode avoids a 15-25% sag on sustained runs (single blog source).

Wired-limit sysctl key differs by macOS: current iogpu.wired_limit_mb, older debug.iogpu.wired_limit; setting a non-existent key silently does nothing; a value of 0 means the default; the setting does not survive reboot.
Models that exceed the working set swap to disk and decode collapses (about 2 vs 9-10 tok/s in one example).

M5 Pro bandwidth: Apple says 307 GB/s. contracollective.com lists 350 and M5 Max 700, M5 Ultra 1400; llmcheck.net says 300/600/1200. The Apple figures win. The contracollective table (M5 Pro 61 / Max 118 / Ultra 214 tok/s on an 8B 4-bit model) is unverified and inconsistent with Apple's bandwidth.

MLX vs llama.cpp: starmorph.com (citing Groundy) says MLX leads 20-87% under ~14B on M4 Max (Qwen3-8B 4-bit: 93.3 vs 76.9) and the gap collapses to a tie at 27B+. local-llm.net says the two tie at 1-7B and MLX leads 10-20% at 14B+. The two sources disagree on where the gap sits; neither is a primary benchmark.

M5 Max vs M4 Max decode gain: llmcheck.net first claimed ~28% from "lab tests", then on 2026-09-23 corrected to an index estimate of 7-10% consistent with the 11% bandwidth gap (614 vs 546 GB/s). Prefer the corrected figure.
M3 Max vs M4 Pro for LLMs (heyuan110.com): M3 Max (300-400 GB/s) beats M4 Pro (273). The llama.cpp table agrees (66.31 vs 50.74 Q4_0 tg).

Effective-throughput framing: famstack.dev reports MLX at 8.5K context on M1 Max spent 94% of wall time in prefill (49.4 s vs GGUF 37.8 s), so a high decode tok/s number hides slow wall-clock on long prompts.
Independent MLX (not llama.cpp) decode measurements on M5 Pro / M5 Max / M5 Ultra for dense 27-70B models.
Why Ultra-tier decode efficiency is only 40-55% on small models (die-to-die fabric, scheduling, or software) and whether it improves with new builds as on M2 Ultra.
Whether M5 Ultra is a dual-die or quad-die part: pinggy.io claims two bonded dual-die M5 Max chips (4.4 TB/s fabric), Apple's newsroom text does not say.
Sustained thermal behavior of MacBook Pro M5 Max versus Mac Studio, measured.
Exact default GPU wired fraction by RAM size (sources say ~2/3 for 32GB, ~75% on larger).
Apple lists M5 Pro at 307 GB/s and M5 Max at up to 614 GB/s with up to 128GB unified memory.
M5 Max with a 32-core GPU has 460 GB/s; the 40-core GPU version has 614 GB/s.
M5 Pro and M5 Max use Apple's Fusion Architecture, combining two dies into one SoC.
Apple's M5 Pro/Max "up to 4x" AI claim is for LLM prompt processing versus M4 Pro/Max, not decode.

Apple announced Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra on 2026-08-25 (pre-order same day, availability September 22): M5 Ultra has up to 80 GPU cores, 36 CPU cores, up to 512GB unified memory and 1.2 TB/s bandwidth, 50 percent higher than before.
Apple claims up to 10.7x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio for Mac Studio M5 Ultra versus M1 Max and 3.9x versus M4 Max; these are prefill figures.
Mac Studio supports Thunderbolt 5 RDMA clustering; Apple says four systems give up to 3x faster inference than one.
The M5 Ultra 512GB configuration ships late October 2026 while other configurations ship September 22.
M4 base is 120 GB/s with up to 32GB unified memory; M4 Pro and Max raised bandwidth up to 75% over the prior generation.
M4 Pro has 273 GB/s; M4 Max has 546 GB/s at 40 GPU cores and about 410 GB/s at 32 GPU cores.
M3 Pro has 150 GB/s versus 200 GB/s for M1 Pro and M2 Pro; the binned M3 Max has 300 GB/s versus 400 for the full part.
The llama.cpp discussion #4167 table gives Q4_0 7B tg128: M1 14.19, M1 Pro 36.41, M1 Max 61.19, M1 Ultra 83.73 tok/s.
Same table: M2 21.91, M2 Pro 38.86, M2 Max 65.95, M2 Ultra 94.27 tok/s (Q4_0 tg128, 2023 build).
Same table: M3 Pro 30.74, M3 Max-300 56.58, M3 Max-400 66.31, M3 Ultra (80-core) 92.14 tok/s.
Same table: M4 24.11, M4 Pro 50.74, M4 Max-410 69.95, M4 Max-546 83.06 tok/s.
Same table, newer build: M5 31.88, M5 Pro 67.59, M5 Max-614 119.92, M5 Ultra-80-core 179.10, M6 35.74 tok/s (Q4_0 tg128).
The same table gives F16 tg128: M4 Max-546 31.64, M5 Pro 21.55, M5 Max 37.11, M5 Ultra 73.60, M3 Ultra-80 39.78 tok/s.
M5 Ultra prompt processing pp512 is 4944.66 (Q4_0) versus 3219.99 for M5 Max and 1620.64 for M5 Pro.
Q4_0 decode efficiency (measured tg / (BW / 3.8 GB)) is 69-84% on base and Pro chips, 58-74% on Max chips, and 40-55% on Ultra chips.
Decode does not scale linearly with bandwidth on the small test model: M5 Ultra gives 1.49x M5 Max for 2x bandwidth, M4 Max-546 gives 1.64x M4 Pro for 2x bandwidth.
The same M2 Ultra improved from 94.27 to 125.21 Q4_0 tg128 tok/s between llama.cpp build 8e672ef (Nov 2023) and c1d0e7a (Aug 2026), a 33% gain.
An M1 Ultra 128GB on build c1d0e7a measured Q4_0 tg128 113.79 tok/s, versus 83.73 on the 2023 build.
Maintainer ggerganov noted the M5-family rows are missing from the old-build comparison; a contributor argued new-build M5 rows are not comparable to old-build M1-M4 rows.
A 256GB Mac Studio M5 Ultra (36-core CPU, 80-core GPU) was benchmarked on 2026-09-30 with llama.cpp v0.3.0 on macOS 27.0.1.
Apple's MLX test (M5 vs M4 24GB MacBook Pro) shows TTFT speedup 3.33-4.06x and generation speedup 1.19-1.27x across six models.
On M3 Ultra 512GB with MLX, Qwen 32B Q4 decode falls from 31.2 tok/s at 1K context to 19.0 at 32K and 8.5 at 128K.
On M3 Ultra, Qwen 32B F16 decode is 10.4 tok/s at 1K and 5.5 at 128K; at 128K Q2 is only 1.7x F16 versus 4.6x at 1K.
On M3 Ultra, Mixtral 8x7B Q4 decodes at 68.4 tok/s at 1K and 46.7 at 32K, versus 31.2 and 19.0 for dense Qwen 32B Q4.
Prefill time on M3 Ultra is compute-bound and nearly identical across Q2/Q4/Q8 (Llama 405B about 10 min at 16K context).
The benchmark author estimates M3 Ultra at about 54 TFLOPS FP16 and TTFT ~ 2 x params x context / TFLOPS.
Measured on M3 Ultra, GLM-5.2 (743B MoE) decodes at 17.7 tok/s, DeepSeek V3 just over 20, dense Llama 405B 2.9.
Streaming a model larger than memory from SSD through llama.cpp mmap runs at 1-2 tok/s.
MLX prefill throughput fell from about 345 tok/s at 1K to 154 tok/s at 128K in the M3 Ultra benchmark.
pinggy.io claims M5 Ultra is a quad-die part (two dual-die M5 Max bonded) with 4.4 TB/s die-to-die bandwidth and 1.2 TB/s on both 64-core and 80-core GPU configs.
On a MacBook Pro M5 Max 128GB, vllm-mlx with Qwen3-8B-4bit gives 87 tok/s single stream and 215 tok/s aggregate at 15 concurrent requests (per-request 16 tok/s).
On the same M5 Max, plain mlx-lm with a 0.6B draft model (speculative decoding) reached 107.6 tok/s per request versus 87 for vllm-mlx without speculation.
On M4 Max, Qwen3-8B 4-bit decodes at 93.3 tok/s with MLX versus 76.9 with llama.cpp; Qwen2.5-27B 4-bit is tied at about 14 tok/s.
Ollama 0.19 (2026-03-30) switched its Apple backend to MLX; Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on M4 Max 64GB went from 57.8 to 111.4 tok/s decode, and the MLX backend needs 32GB+ RAM.
Ollama's own benchmark on a Mac mini M4 Pro with Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B showed 130 tok/s on MLX versus 43 on the old llama.cpp backend.
A 40,000-token prompt on an MLX-backed local agent took about 3.5 minutes before the first token in one author's test.
On M1 Max, MLX with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 8.5K context spent 94% of wall time in prefill (49.4 s versus 37.8 s for GGUF).
Low Power Mode can roughly halve LLM inference speed, and High Power Mode avoids a 15-25% throughput sag on sustained runs.
The wired-limit key is iogpu.wired_limit_mb on current macOS and debug.iogpu.wired_limit on older macOS; a key the system lacks silently does nothing and 0 restores the default.
The wired-limit sysctl does not persist across reboot; it can be set at boot by launchd or /etc/sysctl.conf, and leaving 32-64GB of headroom on a 512GB machine is advised.
A 32GB Mac may expose only about 21-24GB (65-75%) to the GPU by default.
The M5 Max decode gain over M4 Max is estimated at 7-10% (600 vs 546 GB/s as cited there), not the 28% first published; llmcheck.net corrected its page on 2026-09-23.
llmcheck.net and contracollective.com list non-Apple bandwidth figures for M5 Pro/Max/Ultra (300/600/1200 and 350/700/1400 GB/s) that conflict with Apple's 307/614/~1228.
Per-chip tok/s tables on llmcheck.net, modelfit.io and llmconfigurator.com are labeled bandwidth-roofline estimates, not measurements.
Mac mini M6 is listed at 170 GB/s, M5 Pro Mac mini at 307 GB/s with up to 64GB.
Apple Silicon M2 Max has a 512-bit memory bus giving 400 GB/s, and M2 Ultra doubles it.
Across five runtimes on M2 Ultra 192GB, MLX gave the highest sustained decode throughput and Ollama lagged in throughput and TTFT.
The M4 Max 128GB was reported at ~100 tok/s on a 30B MoE in a from-scratch inference engine and 127 tok/s on a 24B MoE.
The Mac Studio M5 Max and MacBook Pro 16-inch M5 Max share the same 460/614 GB/s bandwidth; the portable form factor risks thermal throttling, not bandwidth loss.
